topics.title: The economy and its central problems

learn.hook: Every economy, from a village to India, must answer the same three questions every single day: what to make, how to make it, and who gets it.
points: In any society people produce goods and services, exchange them and consume them to meet their needs. But the resources available (land, labour, capital, raw materials) are limited.
Scarcity of resources relative to wants forces every society to choose how to allocate its resources among competing uses.
What to produce and in what quantities: more food or more clothes, more consumer goods or more capital goods, more public services like schools and hospitals?
How to produce: which technique to use. Labour-intensive techniques use more labour; capital-intensive techniques use more machines.
For whom to produce: how the output is distributed among people, i.e. who gets how much.

example.q: A government must decide whether to build a dam using thousands of workers or a few huge machines, and whether its electricity will go to farms or factories. Identify the central problems.
steps: Choosing workers versus machines is 'how to produce' (technique).
Choosing farms versus factories as users is 'for whom to produce'.
Deciding to build a dam rather than something else is 'what to produce'.
example.answer: All three: what, how and for whom to produce.

learn.reallife: India's MGNREGA rural works often use labour-intensive techniques to create jobs, while metro rail projects use tunnel-boring machines: two different answers to 'how to produce'.

games.title: Which central problem?
items: More wheat or more cotton?
Tractors or bullocks for ploughing?
Should the poor get subsidised rice?
More defence goods or more hospitals?

games.title: Central problems
items: Central problems arise because resources are scarce.
With unlimited resources there would be no need to choose.
'How to produce' deals with the choice of technique.
Labour-intensive versus capital-intensive methods.
Rich countries do not face central problems.
Every economy faces scarcity and must choose.
'For whom to produce' is about distribution of output.
It decides who gets how much.
A capital-intensive technique uses relatively more labour.
It uses relatively more machines (capital).

quiz.q: The central problems of an economy arise mainly because of:
options: Scarcity of resources with alternative uses
quiz.explain: Limited resources that can be used in many ways force choices.
quiz.mistake: Thinks central problems arise only from lack of money

quiz.q: Deciding between labour-intensive and capital-intensive techniques is the problem of:
quiz.explain: Choice of technique is 'how to produce'.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up what and how

quiz.q: Deciding how national output is distributed among households is the problem of:
quiz.explain: Distribution of output is 'for whom'.
quiz.mistake: Confuses distribution with technique

quiz.q: A country deciding whether to produce more consumer goods or more capital goods faces the problem of:
quiz.explain: Choosing the mix of goods is 'what to produce'.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is about technique

quiz.q: A road can be built by 200 workers in 50 days, or by 40 workers with machines in 25 days. How many worker-days does the labour-intensive method use?
quiz.explain: 200 workers × 50 days = 10,000 worker-days (the machine method uses 40 × 25 = 1,000).
steps: Labour-intensive: 200 × 50 = 10,000 worker-days
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the wrong pair of numbers

quiz.q: Which is an example of a capital-intensive technique?
options: Harvesting wheat with a combine harvester
Building a wall by hand with many masons
quiz.explain: A combine harvester replaces a lot of labour with machinery.
quiz.mistake: Picks a method that relies mainly on workers

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Every economy must decide what, how and for whom to produce.
Reason (R): Resources are limited relative to wants in every economy.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Universal scarcity is why every economy faces these problems.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only poor economies face central problems

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the central problems of an economy?
quiz.explain: The three central problems concern production and distribution of goods.
quiz.mistake: Treats any social decision as a central problem

teach.ask: Gappu's forest council must decide: build nests or gather food, use beaks or tools, and give food to which birds? 'What are these problems called?'
teach.praise: Tweet! What, how and for whom to produce: the three central problems, all because resources are scarce!
teach.nudge: Good! You named one problem. What about choosing the method, and deciding who gets the output?

learn.hook: With a fixed farm, a farmer can grow lots of corn, lots of cotton, or some of both. Draw all the best-possible combinations and you get a curve that sums up scarcity.
points: Production possibility set: all combinations of two goods that can be produced with the given resources and technology.
Production possibility frontier (PPF): the combinations obtained when resources are fully and efficiently used. Producing more of one good then means producing less of the other.
A point inside the PPF means resources are under-utilised or wasted (e.g. unemployment, idle factories).
A point outside the PPF is unattainable with the current resources and technology.
The PPF is drawn with one good on each axis and is usually concave (bowed out) to the origin.

example.q: A PPF passes through (corn 2, cotton 7). Classify the points (2, 5) and (2, 9).
steps: At corn = 2, the maximum cotton possible is 7.
(2, 5): less cotton than possible → inside the PPF → under-used resources.
(2, 9): more than possible → outside the PPF → unattainable.

learn.reallife: During the 2020 lockdown, many factories and workers were idle, so India's output moved to a point well inside its PPF.

games.title: Inside, on or outside the PPF?
items: Factories idle due to a strike
All resources fully and efficiently used
A combination needing more resources than exist
Widespread unemployment
Maximum cotton for a given amount of corn
Output beyond current technology

games.title: PPF basics
items: Points on the PPF show full and efficient use of resources.
That is how the frontier is defined.
A point inside the PPF is unattainable.
Inside points are attainable but wasteful.
Points outside the PPF cannot be reached with current resources.
They need more resources or better technology.
The production possibility set includes points inside and on the PPF.
It contains every attainable combination.
Unemployment pushes an economy outside its PPF.
It puts the economy inside the PPF.

quiz.q: The production possibility frontier shows combinations of two goods when:
options: Resources are fully and efficiently used
quiz.explain: Each point on the PPF uses all resources efficiently.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the PPF includes wasteful points

quiz.q: A point inside the PPF indicates:
quiz.explain: More of one or both goods could be produced with the same resources.
quiz.mistake: Confuses inside points with outside points

quiz.q: A point lying outside the PPF is:
options: Unattainable with current resources and technology
quiz.explain: It needs more resources or better technology.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any point can be reached with effort

quiz.q: A PPF passes through (4, 0), (3, 4), (2, 7), (1, 9) and (0, 10), where the first number is corn and the second is cotton. Is (2, 6) inside, on or outside the frontier?
quiz.explain: With corn = 2, up to 7 cotton is possible; producing only 6 means resources are under-used.
quiz.mistake: Compares the wrong coordinates

quiz.q: Using the same PPF, how much cotton is lost if production moves from (2, 7) to (2, 6)?
quiz.explain: Cotton falls from 7 to 6 while corn stays at 2: 1 unit of cotton is wasted.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the inside point loses nothing

quiz.q: Which situation would place an economy inside its PPF?
options: A long strike that shuts many factories
quiz.explain: Idle resources mean actual output is below potential.
quiz.mistake: Confuses idle resources with growth

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): An economy cannot produce at a point outside its PPF.
Reason (R): The PPF shows the maximum output possible with given resources and technology.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Since the PPF is the maximum, anything beyond it cannot be produced right now.
quiz.mistake: Thinks effort alone can exceed the PPF

quiz.q: The production possibility set consists of:
options: Only the points on the PPF
All points on and inside the PPF
quiz.explain: Every combination that can be produced, efficiently or not.
quiz.mistake: Equates the set with the frontier alone

teach.ask: Gappu's forest can make nests or gather berries. 'What does the PPF show? And what if some birds are lazy?'
teach.praise: Tweet! On the PPF all birds work efficiently, inside means lazy birds and waste, outside is impossible for now!
teach.nudge: Good! What happens if some birds stay idle? Where would the forest be compared with the PPF?

topics.title: Opportunity cost and the shape of the PPF

learn.hook: Moving land from cotton to corn is easy at first, using land that is better for corn. Push further and you must give up ever more cotton for each extra unit of corn.
points: Opportunity cost of a good: the amount of the other good that must be given up to produce one more unit of it.
Marginal opportunity cost along a PPF is also called the marginal rate of transformation (MRT): MRT = units of good Y given up ÷ extra units of good X gained.
MRT usually increases as more of one good is produced, because resources are not equally suited to both goods.
Increasing opportunity cost (increasing MRT) makes the PPF concave (bowed out) to the origin. Constant opportunity cost would give a straight-line PPF.
The slope of the PPF (in absolute value) equals the MRT.

example.q: Corn: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4; Cotton: 10, 9, 7, 4, 0. Find the opportunity cost of each extra unit of corn.
steps: 0 → 1 corn: cotton falls 10 → 9, cost 1
1 → 2 corn: 9 → 7, cost 2
2 → 3 corn: 7 → 4, cost 3
3 → 4 corn: 4 → 0, cost 4
example.answer: 1, 2, 3, 4 units of cotton: rising opportunity cost, so the PPF is concave

learn.reallife: If India shifts land from rice to sugarcane in Maharashtra, the first hectares moved may be well suited to sugarcane, but later ones are better rice land, so each extra tonne of sugarcane costs more rice.

items.q: Cotton falls 9 → 7 for 1 more corn. MRT?
Cotton falls 20 → 14 for 2 more corn. MRT?
Guns 0 → 1 lowers butter 50 → 45. Cost of 1 gun?
Y falls 30 → 20 as X rises 5 → 7. MRT?
Cotton falls 4 → 0 for 1 more corn. MRT?
Wheat falls 100 → 85 for 3 more cloth. MRT?

games.title: Match the PPF idea
pairs: Units of the other good given up
Resources not equally efficient in both goods

quiz.q: Opportunity cost of producing one more unit of corn is:
options: The amount of cotton given up to produce it
quiz.explain: It is measured by the alternative output forgone.
quiz.mistake: Equates opportunity cost with the money price

quiz.q: Corn: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4; Cotton: 10, 9, 7, 4, 0. What is the opportunity cost of the 3rd unit of corn?
quiz.explain: Moving from 2 to 3 corn reduces cotton from 7 to 4: 3 units of cotton.
steps: Cotton at 2 corn = 7, at 3 corn = 4
quiz.mistake: Reads the cotton level instead of the change

quiz.q: In the same table (Corn 0–4, Cotton 10, 9, 7, 4, 0), what is the MRT when corn rises from 3 to 4 units?
quiz.explain: Cotton falls from 4 to 0, so MRT = 4.
quiz.mistake: Uses the previous step's MRT

quiz.q: Increasing marginal opportunity cost makes the PPF:
quiz.explain: A rising MRT means the curve bows outward.
quiz.mistake: Confuses concave and convex

quiz.q: If the opportunity cost of one good in terms of the other were constant, the PPF would be:
quiz.explain: A constant slope gives a straight line.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every PPF must be curved

quiz.q: When good X rises from 5 to 7 units, good Y falls from 30 to 20 units. Find the MRT.
quiz.explain: MRT = ΔY/ΔX = 10/2 = 5.
quiz.mistake: Uses only the fall in Y without dividing by the rise in X

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A PPF is usually concave to the origin.
Reason (R): As more of one good is produced, resources less suited to it must be used, so MRT rises.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Rising MRT due to imperfectly adaptable resources gives the bowed-out shape.
quiz.mistake: Knows the shape but not the reason

quiz.q: The slope of the PPF at any point measures:
quiz.explain: Its (absolute) slope is the MRT, the rate at which one good is converted into the other.
quiz.mistake: Confuses MRT with MRS from consumer theory

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If my forest makes one more nest, how many berries do we lose? And why does it get worse each time?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Each extra nest costs more berries because resources aren't equally good at both, so MRT rises and the PPF is concave!
teach.nudge: Good! But why does the cost keep rising? Think about whether all birds are equally good at both jobs.

topics.title: Shifts and rotations of the PPF

learn.hook: The Green Revolution let Indian farmland grow far more wheat and rice than before. In PPF language, it pushed the frontier outward.
points: The PPF is drawn for given resources and technology. If these change, the PPF moves.
Growth of resources (more labour, more capital, new mineral finds) or general improvement in technology shifts the whole PPF outward (to the right).
Loss of resources (war, earthquake, epidemic deaths) shifts the PPF inward (to the left).
If technology improves for only one good, the PPF rotates: its intercept on that good's axis moves out, while the intercept on the other axis stays the same.
An economy moving from inside the PPF to a point on it (e.g. reducing unemployment) is NOT a shift; the PPF itself is unchanged.

example.q: A PPF between cloth and wheat. A new high-yield wheat seed is invented. What happens?
steps: Only wheat production capability improves.
The maximum wheat (if all resources go to wheat) increases.
The maximum cloth stays the same.
example.answer: The PPF rotates outward along the wheat axis, pivoting on the cloth intercept.

learn.reallife: ISRO's satellite-based weather forecasting helps farmers reduce crop losses; better technology like this can push the economy's PPF outward over time.

games.title: Shift, rotation or movement?
items: Increase in the labour force
A major earthquake destroys factories
New technology only in cloth production
Discovery of new mineral deposits
War destroys capital stock
High-yield seed improves only rice output

games.title: PPF movements
items: Better technology for both goods shifts the PPF outward.
More of both can now be produced.
Reducing unemployment shifts the PPF outward.
It moves the economy from inside to onto the existing PPF.
An improvement in technology for one good rotates the PPF.
Only that good's intercept changes.
Loss of resources due to a natural disaster shifts the PPF inward.
Fewer resources mean less potential output.
The PPF stays fixed even if resources grow.
Growth in resources shifts it outward.

quiz.q: An increase in the stock of capital and labour in an economy will:
options: Move the economy inside the PPF
quiz.explain: More resources raise the maximum possible output of both goods.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only technology shifts the PPF

quiz.q: A severe earthquake destroys many factories. The PPF will:
quiz.explain: Loss of resources reduces productive capacity.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it only moves the economy inside the PPF

quiz.q: New technology improves only the production of wheat (on the x-axis). The PPF will:
options: Rotate outward on the wheat axis, keeping the other intercept fixed
quiz.explain: Only the maximum wheat output increases.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any technology change shifts the whole PPF

quiz.q: Government schemes put unemployed workers back to work. On a PPF diagram, this is shown as:
options: An outward shift of the PPF
A movement from a point inside the PPF towards the PPF
quiz.explain: The resources already existed; they are now being used.
quiz.mistake: Confuses using idle resources with gaining new resources

quiz.q: A PPF has maximum outputs of 100 cloth or 50 wheat. A wheat-only technology raises maximum wheat by 20%. What is the new maximum wheat output?
quiz.explain: 50 × 1.2 = 60; maximum cloth stays at 100.
steps: New max wheat = 50 × (1 + 20/100)
quiz.mistake: Applies the increase to cloth or adds 20 directly

quiz.q: Which event shifts the PPF outward?
quiz.explain: New resources raise potential output.
quiz.mistake: Picks an event that wastes or destroys resources

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Economic growth is shown by an outward shift of the PPF.
Reason (R): Growth increases the economy's capacity to produce goods and services.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Higher productive capacity means a bigger set of attainable combinations.
quiz.mistake: Thinks growth only moves the economy along the PPF

quiz.q: Which of these does NOT shift the PPF?
options: Moving resources from wheat to cloth production
quiz.explain: Re-allocating existing resources only moves the economy along the same PPF.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any change in output mix shifts the PPF

teach.ask: Gappu's forest learnt a faster way to weave nests, but berry-picking is unchanged. 'What happens to our PPF?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Technology for nests only rotates the PPF outward on the nest axis. More resources would shift it outward!
teach.nudge: Good! Does the berry maximum change too? What happens to the nest maximum?

topics.title: Organisation of economic activities: planned, market and mixed

learn.hook: In a market economy, no minister decides how many samosas a city needs, yet there are always enough. Prices do the coordinating.
points: Centrally planned economy: the government (central authority) makes the major decisions about what, how and for whom to produce, aiming at the society's overall welfare.
Market economy: economic activities are organised through the market. A market is any arrangement where people can freely buy and sell goods; it need not be a physical place (online platforms count).
In a market economy, prices act as signals: if demand for a good rises, its price tends to rise, which encourages producers to supply more of it.
Mixed economy: both the market and the government play important roles; the government steps in where markets fail (e.g. defence, public health, help for the poor). India is a mixed economy.

example.q: Demand for electric scooters rises sharply in Bengaluru. How does a market economy respond, with no central order?
steps: Higher demand pushes up the price and profits of e-scooters.
Firms are attracted to produce more and new firms enter.
Output rises to meet demand: prices have coordinated the decision.
example.answer: Price signals lead producers to supply more e-scooters.

learn.reallife: In India, prices of most goods are set in markets, but the government runs the Public Distribution System, Indian Railways and public hospitals: a mixed economy at work.

games.title: Which type of economy?
items: Government decides all output targets
Prices alone coordinate production
Private firms plus government-run railways and hospitals
Central authority allocates goods to households
Buyers and sellers freely exchange at market prices
India's economic system

games.title: Organising an economy
items: A market must be a physical place like a mandi.
Any arrangement for free buying and selling, including online, is a market.
In a market economy, a rise in demand tends to raise price and supply.
Prices act as signals.
In a centrally planned economy, the government makes the key decisions.
A central authority plans production and distribution.
India is a purely planned economy.
India is a mixed economy.
In a mixed economy, both markets and the government have important roles.
That is its defining feature.

quiz.q: In a centrally planned economy, the central problems are solved by:
quiz.explain: The central authority decides what, how and for whom.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with a market economy

quiz.q: In a market economy, the main coordinating mechanism is:
quiz.explain: Prices signal what buyers want and guide producers.
quiz.mistake: Thinks government directs a market economy

quiz.q: A market, in economics, means:
options: Any arrangement where buyers and sellers can freely exchange goods
quiz.explain: It need not be a place; online platforms are markets too.
quiz.mistake: Takes the everyday meaning of 'market'

quiz.q: If demand for a good increases in a market economy, its price tends to:
quiz.explain: Rising price raises profitability and induces producers to supply more.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the price signal

quiz.q: India's economy is best described as a:
quiz.explain: Both the market and the government have significant roles.
quiz.mistake: Ignores either the market or the state

quiz.q: Which is a role of the government in a mixed economy?
options: Fixing the price of every single good
quiz.explain: The state supplies public goods and corrects market failures, while markets handle most goods.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a mixed economy is fully planned

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Prices act as signals in a market economy.
Reason (R): A rise in the price of a good indicates greater scarcity or demand, guiding producers to supply more.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Price changes carry information that steers production decisions.
quiz.mistake: Does not see how prices carry information

quiz.q: Online shopping platforms where buyers and sellers never meet face to face are:
options: Not markets because there is no physical place
Markets, because buyers and sellers can freely exchange
quiz.explain: The economic meaning of a market does not require a physical place.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a market must be a building or street

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Who decides how many nests to build in a forest? Is it the eagle chief, the market, or both?'
teach.praise: Tweet! The chief decides in a planned economy, prices decide in a market economy, and both share the job in a mixed economy like India!
teach.nudge: Good! What guides decisions when there is no chief? And what do we call a system where both work together?

topics.title: Positive vs normative economics, micro vs macro

learn.hook: 'Petrol prices rose 5% last year' can be checked with data. 'Petrol should be cheaper' is a judgement. Economists keep the two apart.
points: Positive economics describes how economic mechanisms actually work: what is, was or will be. Its statements can be tested with facts.
Normative economics evaluates whether outcomes are desirable: what ought to be. Its statements involve value judgements (often using 'should', 'ought to').
Microeconomics studies individual economic agents (consumers, firms) and how prices and quantities are determined in individual markets.
Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole: aggregate output, employment, the general price level, growth and inflation.

example.q: Classify: (a) 'A rise in onion prices reduces quantity demanded.' (b) 'The government should give free electricity to farmers.' (c) 'India's GDP growth rate rose last year.'
steps: (a) Testable cause and effect in one market: positive, micro.
(b) A value judgement with 'should': normative.
(c) A testable fact about the whole economy: positive, macro.

learn.reallife: The RBI's study of how a repo-rate change affects inflation is macroeconomics; a study of how a tomato price rise affects tomato demand is microeconomics.

games.title: Positive or normative?
items: Unemployment in India rose last year

quiz.q: Positive economics deals with:
options: What is, was or will be
quiz.explain: It describes actual economic mechanisms and can be tested.
quiz.mistake: Confuses positive with normative

quiz.q: Which statement is normative?
options: The government should provide free education to all
A fall in price raises quantity demanded
quiz.explain: 'Should' signals a value judgement.
quiz.mistake: Treats a factual statement as normative

quiz.q: Which statement is positive?
options: Taxes on the rich ought to be higher
The price of petrol rose by ₹2 per litre last month
quiz.explain: It is a factual claim that can be checked.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any statement about prices is normative

quiz.q: Microeconomics studies:
quiz.explain: It focuses on individual agents and individual markets.
quiz.mistake: Confuses micro with macro

quiz.q: Which of these is a macroeconomic topic?
options: Price of a single brand of shoes
quiz.explain: Unemployment in the whole economy is an aggregate.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any big market is macro

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): 'A rise in income increases demand for normal goods' is a positive statement.
Reason (R): It can be tested against facts.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Testability with data makes it positive.
quiz.mistake: Thinks economic theories are normative

quiz.q: Of 10 statements in a test, 4 use 'should' or 'ought' and the rest are factual. How many are positive statements?
quiz.explain: 10 − 4 = 6 factual (positive) statements.
quiz.mistake: Counts the normative ones instead

quiz.q: The study of how the price of rice is determined in a market is part of:
quiz.explain: Price determination in an individual market is a microeconomic topic.
quiz.mistake: Thinks anything about food is macro

teach.ask: Gappu argues: 'Berries got costlier last month, and the forest should make them free!' Are both statements the same type? Teach me!
teach.praise: Tweet! 'Costlier' is positive, a testable fact. 'Should be free' is normative, a value judgement!
teach.nudge: Good! Which statement can be checked with data? Which one is an opinion about what ought to be?
